note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · IS IT AN ANNUAL?
tiles.details: Trace an attached plant downward. Mucronate sprangletop is an annual and can have culms bending at lower nodes. Native green sprangletop (Disakisperma dubium) normally has a robust persistent perennial base. A disconnected flowering branch doesn't prove lifespan.
tiles.short: Slender, fibrous-rooted grass; no lasting perennial crown

tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE FINGERS
tiles.details: The flower head can look like a narrow brush with numerous slender, nearly straight branches inserted at separate positions. The newly archived Bob Harms photographs are of the different subsp. brachiata; use them to learn shared architecture, NOT to confirm subsp. mucronata.
tiles.short: Many fine side racemes distributed along a long central axis

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE LEAF
tiles.details: NEW direct photo 190322lg by Jim Conrad from source-labelled ssp. mucronata visibly separates the whitish ragged membranous ligule at leaf blade/sheath junction from long white sheath hairs BELOW; both have explicit accurate broad arrows. This original lacks a ruler: do not infer measured ligule height or minute bulbous hair insertion.
tiles.short: Check short membranous ligule AND raised-base sheath hairs

tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT THE FLORETS
tiles.details: A mature 2–4 mm Dinebra panicea complex spikelet often contains 2–4 florets. Under 20× follow the upper glume to its tiny mucro (short firm point), count REAL florets within one spikelet, and compare glumes against fertile florets. Subspecies separation requires mature glumes/fruit on correctly vouchered specimen; don't promote species-complex photo to exact mucronata. Real Jim Conrad subspecies-determined Yucatan source photo is now archived with a TRUE ruler next to attached spikelets. Use photo panel 2 to see actual size, but do not identify an individual glume-tip mucro from that image.
tiles.short: Tiny multi-flowered spikelets; verify glume tips and pedicel

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT GLUMES, LEMMAS AND TINY TIP
tiles.details: On a correctly source-determined subsp. mucronata specimen, use 20–40× and a real 1-mm reference to separate both glumes from each floret's lemma and palea. A published regional comparison mentions fertile lemma body around 0.9–1.2 mm; confirm with a treatment and measured voucher before using that as a subspecies threshold. Inspect the minute firm UPPER-GLUME mucro at its actual tip, not an invented long lemma awn. Jim Conrad's real rulered Yucatán target-subspecies spikelets show size but do NOT resolve the tiny mucro or individual lemma insertion.
tiles.short: ~2–4 mm mature spikelet; usually 2–4 florets; check the UPPER glume's minute mucro.

tiles.heading: 06 · LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLIC-READY GATE
tiles.details: Compare D. panicea subsp. brachiata at matched mature glume/lemma scale: the four credited Bob Harms Central Texas plates are DIFFERENT-subspecies comparisons. Green sprangletop (Disakisperma dubium) is generally a larger perennial with 4–12 mm, 4–13-flowered spikelets; overlapping 4-floret counts are not decisive. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: locally documented rooted annual and attached full panicle, 1-mm true ligule, actual raised sheath-hair bases, 20–40× glume-tip mucro, dissected lemma/palea and matched subspecies voucher. NEEDS_SITE_QA: seven archived photo records and source/rights/labels, four existing exact-target broad arrows, non-CC Harms educational attribution, mobile tile/arrow rendering and deployed site. Never certify the subspecies or FINISHED from unverified microanatomy.
tiles.short: Do not mistake subsp. brachiata photos for this target; retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP (subsp. mucronata) — annual with many slender ascending branches along a central axis and 2–4(-5)-flowered tiny spikelets. Short truncate/irregular membranous true ligule and raised-base sheath hairs must be inspected on the target itself. Four Central Texas Bob Harms comparison images show DIFFERENT subspecies brachiata, not a confirmed mucronata; the two separately labelled native green sprangletop photographs show larger multi-flowered units. Do not equate species complex or background other subspecies with target.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START at target panel 1 (index 0): look for many fine ascending flowering branches on a slender annual. The original photograph does NOT show a connected rooted base; an annual life cycle cannot be proved from a clipped stem.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: NEW direct photo 190322lg by Jim Conrad from source-labelled ssp. mucronata visibly separates the whitish ragged membranous ligule at leaf blade/sheath junction from long white sheath hairs BELOW; both have explicit accurate broad arrows. This original lacks a ruler: do not infer measured ligule height or minute bulbous hair insertion.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On a correctly source-determined subsp. mucronata specimen, use 20–40× and a real 1-mm reference to separate both glumes from each floret's lemma and palea. A published regional comparison mentions fertile lemma body around 0.9–1.2 mm; confirm with a treatment and measured voucher before using that as a subspecies threshold. Inspect the minute firm UPPER-GLUME mucro at its actual tip, not an invented long lemma awn. Jim Conrad's real rulered Yucatán target-subspecies spikelets show size but do NOT resolve the tiny mucro or individual lemma insertion.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: GREEN SPRANGLETOP / Disakisperma dubium: generally a larger perennial arising from a lasting base, commonly with fewer longer near-fingerlike branches, and larger 4–12 mm spikelets containing about 4–13 florets. MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP / Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata: slender ANNUAL with many ascending slender branches, generally much smaller ~2–4 mm spikelets with ~2–4 florets and often bulbous-based sheath hairs. Counts can overlap at 4 florets, so a single spikelet count isn't decisive. ERAGROSTIS lovegrasses: many have an airy panicle too but individual spikelets have several fertile florets in overlapping ranks, and the branching/spikelet anatomy differs. Within DINEBRA, the other subspecies of D. panicea can look extremely similar; a photograph labeled merely Dinebra panicea is NOT independently sufficient to certify subsp. mucronata. Old Leptochloa mucronata refers to this taxon in the Kew treatment; Leptochloa filiformis and other older names have been applied differently in historical treatments.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: TARGET MUCRONATA: actual spikelets beside real mm ruler — Jim Conrad, Yucatan (two arrows)
panels.caption: AUTHENTIC original Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata (as Leptochloa panicea ssp. mucronata), Jim Conrad, Yucatan, March 2019. On the left is a real diagonal millimeter ruler; on the right, individual small spikelets REMAIN ATTACHED to a slender raceme branch. Two gross-region arrows point to those visible features. The original account identifies the actual subspecies, unlike the four nearby Harms comparison photos of subsp. brachiata. The actual UPPER GLUME TINY MUCRO is NOT independently resolved, and it is not a Texas voucher. Public domain by creator's express dedication.

panels.label: TRUE MUCRONATA LEAF COLLAR · jagged ligule vs separate white sheath hairs (two arrows)
panels.caption: REAL source-labelled D. panicea subsp. mucronata (Jim Conrad, Yucatan 2019, original Leptochloa name). The upward projecting PALE, ragged-edged membranous LIGULE lies at the true inner leaf blade–sheath junction; the conspicuous LONG WHITE HAIRS are ON THE SHEATH BELOW, not themselves the ligule. The two broad arrows distinguish those visible structures. This image has NO millimeter ruler, and does NOT independently reveal individual swollen/papilla hair insertion points. It is NOT a Hays voucher. Photographer dedicated his own images to public domain.

panels.label: DIFFERENT NATIVE GREEN SPRANGLETOP · ATTACHED SPIKELETS: actual regional multi-flowered close-up
panels.caption: OTHER SPECIES, Disakisperma dubium, NOT Dinebra. Jim Conrad Uvalde photograph of two true attached green sprangletop spikelets. Do not count all floral scales as separate spikelets; florets are INSIDE a single spikelet. Source's two preverified arrows are kept on its actual structures. Native perennial typically has larger multi-flowered spikelets, useful contrast against a Dinebra ANNUAL; no absolute one-character ID.

intro: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP (subsp. mucronata) — annual with many slender ascending branches along a central axis and 2–4(-5)-flowered tiny spikelets. Short truncate/irregular membranous true ligule and raised-base sheath hairs must be inspected on the target itself. Four Central Texas Bob Harms comparison images show DIFFERENT subspecies brachiata, not a confirmed mucronata; the two separately labelled native green sprangletop photographs show larger multi-flowered units. Do not equate species complex or background other subspecies with target.
memory_rule: MANY THIN BRANCHES + ANNUAL BASE + TINY USUALLY 2–4-FLORET SPIKELETS suggests Dinebra panicea. Subspecies mucronata needs close botanical determination, not an ordinary photo.
safety_note: All seven image records physically exist, but only three are target subspecies. Jim Conrad originals are from Yucatán, not Hays County. The four Bob Harms photographs have credited educational-use-only terms, not Creative Commons. Never label a different subspecies or unresolved mucro as confirmed target anatomy.
field_rule: Many slender ascending branches + tiny multi-flowered spikelets + actual jagged membranous ligule and separate sheath hairs support the Dinebra complex; only verified mature glume/caryopsis characters and voucher context can confirm subsp. mucronata.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
